judgeNotes:
I kept 62 of the 169 extras. I judged them on counts first.

THE BAR, taken from selected.tsv: for selected items judged 3, the median count is 29 and the lower quartile is 11. Every selected item judged 3 with a count under 20 (49 of them) got in on everyday judgement, not on counts. In the full pool, items judged 3 with counts of 10–19 were selected only about 9% of the time. Items judged 4 with counts of 10–20 were selected about half the time. So my count bar was:
- judged 3: at least 20 figurative hits
- judged 4: at least 10
- judged 2: at least 30, and only if the count isn't inflated by drama scenes

I checked counts against the corpus myself (collocations-build/corpus/ja.txt.gz) wherever a literal twin or a pair count could inflate them. Being "covered" by a synonym in the selected list did not count against an extra, because the selected list already holds synonym sets (atama ni kuru / hara ga tatsu / katto naru). Only true variants and single words were dropped on those grounds.

KEPT, with their checked figurative counts:
- About 100 or more: ki ni kakeru 274, ki ga kuruu 247, baka iwanaide 239, chikara o kasu 197, kuchi ni suru 175, chikara o awaseru 123, shitta kotcha nai 112, kokoro o hiraku 107, katte ni shite 100, kokoro no junbi 92.
- Roughly 40–70: issen o koeru, ippiki ookami, hanashi o tsukeru, te o tsukeru, kiku mimi, nukeme, en o kiru, ki o torareru, on ni kiru, ki o hiku, teki ni mawasu, zamaa miro, omoi mo yoranai, sente o utsu, me o somukeru, ohiraki.
- Roughly 20–40: the rest of the list.
- At exactly 20–21, right on the bar: yake ni naru (20 once jibou jiki is excluded), ii ki ni naru, ii dokyou, kimari ga warui, kuchi ni au, kami hitoe, kejime.
- On scope rather than count: katte ni shite is close to katte ni, which is already in the versatility list. chikara o awaseru and kokoro no junbi are close to literal. I kept all three on their counts, but the other judges may weigh scope differently.

DROPPED:
- Count is mostly the literal meaning:
  - me o samasu: 510 hits, almost all "wake up"; me ga sameru is a kept collocation.
  - hone o oru: mostly broken bones.
  - iki ga tsumaru: about half is real choking.
  - myaku ga aru: mostly "no pulse".
  - me ga kuramu: about 18 figurative.
  - nami ni noru: surfing.
  - kidou ni noru: half are orbits.
  - mune ga itamu: chest pain.
  - mune ni te o atete kangaeru: mostly literal.
- Pair counts that overstate the real phrase:
  - aite no mi ni naru: about 5 real hits, not 51.
  - te ga denai: 3 phrase hits.
  - sewa ga yakeru: 7.
  - ooguchi o tataku: about 18.
  - ki ni kakaru: about 22 real hits, and it is ki ni naru again.
- Single words: otagaisama, oteage, yatsuatari suru, inochibiroi suru.
- Variant: me ga hanasenai is a form of the selected me o hanasu.
- Inflated by drama scenes: kuchi o waru (judged 2, crime-scene interrogations).
- Literal (judged 4, but the meaning is just its parts): ichi kara yarinaosu.
- Just under 20: munakuso warui 19, ii kimi 19, mizu o sasu about 17, me o hiku about 18 (mostly hitome o hiku), nagare ni makaseru 18, kokoro ga hiroi 16, atama ni ireru 15, kotsu o tsukamu 12 (also cut from the collocation list).
- Everything else judged 3 with a count under 20, plus kangae ga amai (5) and dotchi mo dotchi (4). Some of these are real casual phrases that the subtitles under-count: isshou no onegai, engi demo nai, ki ga hayai, kenka suru hodo naka ga ii, yoso wa yoso. The counts can't support them, so it's for the everyday judge to make the case for them.

I'm keeping 159 of the 169 extras and cutting 10. To set the bar I looked at the bottom of the selected list, not its median. The selected list has 66 idioms judged 3 with fewer than 30 hits, plus sayings with almost no hits, such as saru mo ki kara ochiru, nido aru koto wa sando aru, oburaato ni tsutsumu and chiri mo tsumoreba. Judged as a native speaker, nearly all the extras are said at least that often, and many are said more: katte ni shite, kokoro no junbi, myaku ga aru, engi demo nai, dotchi mo dotchi, ki ga hayai, isshou no onegai, te ga aku, karada ga motanai, kaya no soto, yoso wa yoso uchi wa uchi. I kept the four-character phrases people say aloud (ichimoku ryouzen, hanshin hangi, shinki itten, tanin gyougi). I also kept fixed two-word metaphors like ippiki ookami, kami hitoe and kekka oorai, because the selected list already has the same kind (mikka bouzu, asameshi mae, aka no tanin). None of the 159 is in the collocation list itself: kuchi ni au and kotsu o tsukamu appear only in its cuts, marked as belonging on the idiom list. Near-synonyms of selected idioms that are common on their own stay in, as the selected list already does for its several 'anger' and 'meddle' idioms: omoi mo yoranai, tachiuchi dekinai, kubi ga tobu, mi kara deta sabi, ki ni kakaru, kokoro koko ni arazu.

CUT (10):
- Single words, out of scope under the rule the task names (otagaisama, tanabota-type words). The meaning sits in one word and suru or o suru adds nothing, which matches the earlier single-word cuts kageguchi o iu and guchi o kobosu:
  - otagaisama (named in the task)
  - oteage
  - yatsuatari-suru
  - inochibiroi-suru
  - shirinugui-o-suru
  All five are common, and a note on a related entry could name them as plain words.
- kuchi-o-waru: a crime-drama line about suspects. It was judged 2 and is rare in everyday talk.
- hone-o-oru: the figurative 'go to trouble for someone' is mostly polite business speech (o-honeori itadaki), and the literal 'break a bone' takes most of its hits. The selected hone ga oreru is the everyday idiom.
- me-ga-iku: close to literal ('your eyes go to it'), only 9 hits, and never judged. The idea is already covered by me ni tsuku and me o hiku.
- me-ga-hanasenai: this is the potential form of the selected me o hanasu, and that entry's notes already teach it. Variants count once.
- uma-ga-au: a near-twin of the selected ki ga au, named in that entry's notes, and said much less (phrase count 5 against 63 for ki ga au).

Borderline extras I kept, ranked by how close they were to being cut: me-o-hikaraseru, ii-dokyou-shiteru, tohou-ni-kureru, mimi-o-utagau, me-o-somukeru, kimari-ga-warui, doji-o-fumu, kuchi-ni-suru (a slightly formal twin of kuchi ni dasu, and the counterpart of the selected mimi ni suru). If the list needs trimming, take these out first. A quirk to flag: the selected list itself holds tanabota and dame moto, which the single-word rule would exclude.

I'm keeping 94 of the 169 extras and dropping 75. I measured the bar against the selected list's own floor. That floor has jc 3 items down to 0–10 hits, kept as corrections for casual talk that subtitles under-count. It also already rejected literal phrases, single words, variant forms and lower-count same-meaning synonyms.

WHY THESE STAY: All 94 are true idioms, fixed phrases or sayings people really say. That includes every scope-clean item in the selector's own list of about 60 near misses (result.json boundaryNotes says they're as common as the bottom of the list). It also includes most of the cut step's "maybe" items.

Two keeps fell between the lists. The collocation list cut kotsu o tsukamu and kuchi ni au with the verdict "idiom, belongs on the idiom list", so they aren't repeats. The judges' note that kotsu o tsukamu was already in the collocation list is wrong: it's only in that list's cuts.

A few judges' "less-common" verdicts are overridden because the counts sit above much of the selected floor and the phrases are everyday: kuchi ga umai (15, completes the kuchi ga katai/karui/warui set), ni no tsugi (18), kaya no soto (13), ichimoku ryouzen (12), dou iu kaze no fukimawashi (10), iki ga tsumaru (30, mostly the "stifling" sense in samples).

DROPPED FOR SCOPE:
- Literal or plain collocations: baka iwanaide, chikara o awaseru, kokoro no junbi, katte ni shite (the versatility list has katte ni), atama ni ireru, atama ni hairanai, ichi kara yarinaosu, kimochi o kirikaeru, karada ga motanai, hito ga kawaru, me ga iku.
- Literal twin: me o samasu. Most of its 525 hits are real waking up, and the collocation list has me ga sameru.
- Single words: otagaisama, oteage, yatsuatari suru, inochibiroi suru.
- Variants or near-duplicates of a selected item:
  - chikara o kasu (te o kasu)
  - kuchi ni suru (kuchi ni dasu)
  - hone o oru (hone ga oreru; most hits are literal broken bones)
  - mimi ni hairu (mimi ni suru)
  - nani ga nan da ka wakaranai (wake ga wakaranai)
  - omoi mo yoranai (yume ni mo omowanai)
  - ki ni kakaru (ki ni naru)
  - tachiuchi dekinai (ha ga tatanai)
  - me ga hanasenai (me o hanasu)
  - ii ki ni naru (choushi ni noru)
  - nagare ni makaseru (naru you ni naru)
  - ii dokyou shiteru (yoku iu yo)
  - me o hiku (me ni tsuku)
  - shika atama ni nai (atama kara hanarenai / atama ga ippai)
  - kubi ga tobu (kubi ni naru)
  - uma ga au (ki ga au; 5 hits against 63)
  - oujougiwa ga warui (akirame ga warui)
  - mi kara deta sabi (jigou jitoku)
  - rui wa tomo o yobu (nita mono doushi)
  - kokoro koko ni arazu (uwa no sora, and literary)
  - ki ga hareru (ki ga sumu / ki ga raku / ki ga magireru)
- Bookish, narrow or drama-only: tohou ni kureru, kuchi o waru, ohiraki ni suru, me o hikaraseru, mi ni oboe ga nai, mimi o utagau, shinki itten, nodo kara te ga deru hodo hoshii.

DROPPED AS BELOW THE BAR (low count with no near-miss support): sente o utsu, kidou ni noru, nami ni noru, te ga denai, baka o miru, doji o fumu, jirai o fumu (mostly literal landmines in the corpus), munasawagi ga suru, hotobori ga sameru, hanashi o awaseru, ki ga ki ja nai, ii kao o suru, hanashi ga mienai, kao o tsubusu, kao o tateru, ki ga shirenai, migi kara hidari, ki o mawasu, nen ni wa nen o ireru, utsuwa ga chiisai, kuchi ga sakete mo ienai, me no doku, mono wa iiyou, mono wa kangaeyou, ne mo ha mo nai, te ni tsukanai, hanashi hanbun ni kiku, me ga ten ni naru, kado ga tatsu, mune ni te o atete kangaeru.

CAVEATS FOR THE MERGE:
- Subtitle counts overstate these because English lines get translated into them: issen o koeru ("crossed the line"), ippiki ookami ("lone wolf"), kokoro o hiraku ("open your heart"), ki ga kuruu. They're native idioms too, so they stay, but don't sort them by raw count.
- zamaa miro and ii kimi are both kept. zamaa miro is the rough taunt to someone's face; ii kimi is the milder, more widely usable "serves them right" said about someone else. The merge could fold one into the other's note.
- Keep the flags: rough/casual-only on zamaa miro, munakuso warui and shitta kotcha nai; masculine on on ni kiru.
- Contrast pairs worth wiring up:
  - sewa ga yakeru / te ga kakaru
  - te ga aku / te ga hanasenai
  - kuchi ga umai with the kuchi family
  - kiku mimi o motanai / mimi o kasu
  - ki o torareru / ki ga chiru
  - kejime o tsukeru / keri o tsukeru

vetted.english: it's driving me crazy
vetted.literal: the mind feels about to go haywire
vetted.use: Exaggerated distress, whether frustration (kono oto, ki ga kuruisou), worry, longing or being cooped up (aitakute ki ga kuruisou datta). Ki demo kurutta no? (have you lost your mind?) is mostly a dubbed-film line; in real talk it's atama okashii n ja nai? Ki ga kuruu touches on mental illness, so TV avoids it, and atama ga okashiku narisou is the softer everyday swap.

example.romaji: tonari no kouji, urusakute ki ga kuruisou.
example.ja: 隣の工事、うるさくて気が狂いそう。
example.english: The construction next door is so loud it's driving me crazy.

examplePolite.romaji: hikkoshi to shigoto ga kasanatte, ki ga kuruisou deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 引っ越しと仕事が重なって、気が狂いそうでした。
examplePolite.english: Moving house and work all hit at once. I thought I'd lose my mind.

vetted.notes: Softer: atama ga okashiku narisou. Film line: ki demo kurutta no? = have you lost your mind? (most of the 257 hits are ki ga kurutta / ki demo kurutta; the -sou headword itself is 54).

vetted.english: fine, do what you want
vetted.use: Ends an argument when you give up on persuading someone: mou ii, katte ni shite. The rough male katte ni shiro is the form films use most, and katte ni sureba (go ahead, then) is colder. Douzo gokatte ni is the polite, icy version. Suki ni shite is the friendly 'do as you like'.

example.romaji: mou ii, katte ni shite.
example.ja: もういい、勝手にして。
example.english: Forget it. Do whatever you want.

examplePolite.romaji: wakarimashita. jaa, katte ni shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: わかりました。じゃあ、勝手にしてください。
examplePolite.english: Fine. Suit yourself, then.

vetted.notes: Rough: katte ni shiro (72 of the 107 hits; katte ni shite itself is 15). Colder: katte ni sureba. Polite and icy: douzo gokatte ni.

vetted.kana: こころのじゅんびができる
vetted.english: be emotionally ready
vetted.use: Mostly negative, when news or a big moment comes too fast: mada kokoro no junbi ga dekitenai. Kokoro no junbi wa ii? asks if someone is ready to hear something. Plain junbi ga dekiru is being ready in practical terms.

example.romaji: chotto matte, mada kokoro no junbi ga dekitenai.
example.ja: ちょっと待って、まだ心の準備ができてない。
example.english: Wait, I'm not ready for this yet.

examplePolite.romaji: kyuu ni iwarete mo, mada kokoro no junbi ga dekitenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 急に言われても、まだ心の準備ができてないんです。
examplePolite.english: This is so sudden. I'm just not ready for it yet.

vetted.notes: Also: kokoro no junbi o suru (brace yourself).

vetted.english: serves you right, ha!
vetted.literal: look at the state of you
vetted.use: The stock gloat at someone getting their comeuppance, often said jokingly among friends or muttered at a rival; zamaa! on its own is common too. Ii kimi da is the cooler, more grown-up 'serves them right'.

example.romaji: sakki warikonde kita kuruma, tsukamatteru. zamaa miro.
example.ja: さっき割り込んできた車、捕まってる。ざまあみろ。
example.english: That car that cut in on us got pulled over. Ha, serves him right.

vetted.notes: Also: zamaa!, zama miro.

vetted.english: serves them right
vetted.use: Spiteful satisfaction when someone who had it coming gets hurt, usually ii kimi da, said about them or to their face. It's cooler and more grown-up than the taunting zamaa miro. The kimi here is 'feeling' (as in kimi ga warui), not kimi 'you'.

example.romaji: itsumo ibatteta kara, ii kimi da yo.
example.ja: いつも威張ってたから、いい気味だよ。
example.english: He was always so full of himself, so serves him right.

vetted.english: act recklessly out of despair
vetted.use: Doing something rash and self-destructive after a breakup, a failure or bad news because nothing seems to matter, mostly said about someone: furarete yake ni natteru, yake ni natte zenbu nonjatta. The line you say to them is yake ni naranaide (don't do anything stupid). Tohou ni kureru is being stuck and helpless; yake ni naru is throwing caution to the wind.

example.romaji: ikkai shippai shita kurai de, yake ni naranaide yo.
example.ja: 一回失敗したくらいで、ヤケにならないでよ。
example.english: Don't go off the rails just because you failed once.

examplePolite.romaji: yake ni naranaide, mou ichido kangaete mimashou.
examplePolite.ja: ヤケにならないで、もう一度考えてみましょう。
examplePolite.english: Don't do anything rash. Let's think it over again.

vetted.notes: Different word by ear: the adverb yake ni (awfully, oddly), heard more often: yake ni shizuka da na = it's awfully quiet. yakekuso (desperate, all-or-nothing); yakezake (drinking to drown it).

vetted.english: feel better, the gloom lifts
vetted.literal: the mind clears up (like the sky)
vetted.use: Said after venting, a good cry or a change of scene (hanashitara ki ga hareta), as advice (sanpo demo shitara ki ga hareru yo), or in sore de ki ga hareru nara (if that makes you feel better). Ki ga magireru only takes your mind off a worry for a while; ki ga hareru means it actually lifts.

example.romaji: omoikkiri naitara, chotto ki ga hareta.
example.ja: 思いっきり泣いたら、ちょっと気が晴れた。
example.english: I had a good cry and feel a bit better.

examplePolite.romaji: hanashi o kiite moratte, sukoshi ki ga haremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 話を聞いてもらって、少し気が晴れました。
examplePolite.english: Having you listen made me feel a little better.

vetted.notes: Everyday swap: sukkiri shita. Pick-me-up: kibarashi. Variant: kibun ga hareru.

vetted.english: feel stifled, suffocating
vetted.use: A complaint about a tense or controlling home, office or relationship: ano ie, iki ga tsumaru, often as iki ga tsumarisou. It can also be literal, not being able to breathe.

example.romaji: jikka ni zutto iru to, iki ga tsumaru.
example.ja: 実家にずっといると、息が詰まる。
example.english: Being at my parents' the whole time is suffocating.

examplePolite.romaji: ano kaigi, iki ga tsumarisou deshita.
examplePolite.ja: あの会議、息が詰まりそうでした。
examplePolite.english: That meeting was so tense I could barely breathe.

vetted.notes: Single word: ikigurushii (stifling).

vetted.english: be at a total loss
vetted.literal: night falls on the way ahead
vetted.use: Being stranded with no idea what to do next, mostly as a state and when telling the story afterwards: saifu nakushite tohou ni kureteta. On the spot people just say dou shiyou. It's helpless rather than upset; yake ni naru is giving up and doing something rash.

example.romaji: shuuden nogashite, eki de tohou ni kureteta.
example.ja: 終電逃して、駅で途方に暮れてた。
example.english: I missed the last train and was stuck at the station with no idea what to do.

examplePolite.romaji: saifu o nakushite, tohou ni kurete imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 財布をなくして、途方に暮れていました。
examplePolite.english: I'd lost my wallet and was completely at a loss.

vetted.notes: Not kureru 'give': this kureru is 'grow dark', as in hi ga kureru.

vetted.english: get fed up, be sick of it
vetted.literal: a feeling of dislike creeps in
vetted.englishIdiom: be sick and tired of it
vetted.use: Said about a job, a place, a routine or yourself, often as iyake ga sashite kita (I'm getting sick of it): shigoto ni iyake ga sasu. Akiru is being bored of something; iyake ga sasu is real dislike.

example.romaji: mainichi onaji koto no kurikaeshi de, iyake ga sashite kita.
example.ja: 毎日同じことの繰り返しで、嫌気がさしてきた。
example.english: Same thing every day. I'm getting sick of it.

examplePolite.romaji: shoujiki, ima no shigoto ni iyake ga sashite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 正直、今の仕事に嫌気がさしています。
examplePolite.english: Honestly, I'm fed up with my job.

vetted.notes: Plain word: unzari suru (be fed up).

vetted.english: fret over it, take it to heart
vetted.literal: fall ill in the mind over it
vetted.use: Mostly as comfort to someone blaming themselves: ki ni yamu koto nai yo, ki ni yamanaide, ki ni yamanakute ii yo (don't let it eat at you). It sounds more serious and grown-up than ki ni shinaide. Ki ni suru is everyday minding; ki ni yamu is brooding until it hurts.

example.romaji: anata no sei ja nai n da kara, ki ni yamanaide.
example.ja: あなたのせいじゃないんだから、気に病まないで。
example.english: It's not your fault, so don't beat yourself up over it.

examplePolite.romaji: amari ki ni yamanaide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: あまり気に病まないでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please don't let it weigh on you too much.

vetted.notes: Everyday version: ki ni shinaide.

vetted.english: feel awkward, sheepish
vetted.use: The awkward feeling of being caught out or having to face people after a slip, often in the past: uso ga barete kimari ga warukatta. Batsu ga warui means the same but is said less, and in everyday talk most people just say kimazui; hazukashii is plain embarrassment.

example.romaji: uso ga barete, sugoku kimari ga warukatta.
example.ja: 嘘がバレて、すごくきまりが悪かった。
example.english: My lie got found out and I felt so sheepish.

examplePolite.romaji: ima kara okurete hairu no wa, chotto kimari ga warui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今から遅れて入るのは、ちょっときまりが悪いですね。
examplePolite.english: It's a bit awkward to walk in late now.

vetted.notes: Also said without ga: kimari warui. Everyday word: kimazui (what younger speakers say). Same meaning, rarer: batsu ga warui.

vetted.english: it pains me, it breaks my heart
vetted.use: Said about sad news, someone's hardship, or guilt at hurting someone: aa iu nyuusu o miru to mune ga itamu. Kokoro ga itamu means the same and is said about three times as often; mune ga itamu sounds a little more formal. For guilt, English says 'I feel bad' or 'it pains me' rather than 'it breaks my heart'. Mune ga itai can also be literal chest pain.

example.romaji: aa iu nyuusu o miru to, mune ga itamu yo ne.
example.ja: ああいうニュースを見ると、胸が痛むよね。
example.english: News like that really breaks your heart.

examplePolite.romaji: hisaichi no eizou o miru to, mune ga itamimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 被災地の映像を見ると、胸が痛みます。
examplePolite.english: It breaks my heart to see the footage from the disaster area.

vetted.notes: Same meaning, said more: kokoro ga itamu. Casual: mune ga itai (included in the count; can also be literal chest pain). Written: mune o itameru.

vetted.english: sickening, leaves you disgusted
vetted.use: A rough reaction to a nasty story, an unfair ending or a bully: munakuso warui hanashi da na. Kimochi warui is gut-level 'gross, creepy'; munakuso warui is moral disgust at something unfair or cruel.

example.romaji: ano nyuusu, maji de munakuso warui.
example.ja: あのニュース、マジで胸くそ悪い。
example.english: That news is seriously sickening.

vetted.notes: Slang short form: munakuso.

vetted.english: smooth-talking, good with words (often of flattery or sales talk)
vetted.use: A warning about a salesperson or charmer who talks people round (kuchi ga umai kara ki o tsukete), or a laughing reply to a compliment: mata, kuchi ga umai n da kara. Not umai alone (tasty, good at).

example.romaji: kare, kuchi ga umai kara ki o tsukete.
example.ja: 彼、口がうまいから気をつけて。
example.english: He's a smooth talker, so watch out.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa kuchi ga umai node, ki o tsukete kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は口がうまいので、気をつけてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: He's a smooth talker, so do be careful.

vetted.notes: Also kuchi ga jouzu; written 口が上手い too. To someone's face in polite speech: mata, ojouzu desu ne / okuchi ga ojouzu desu ne.

vetted.english: suit one's taste (food or drink)
vetted.use: The host's line when serving food or drink, politely with o: okuchi ni au ka wakarimasen kedo; the question every visitor to Japan gets: nihon no tabemono, kuchi ni au? (politely okuchi ni aimasu ka?); and a soft way to say you don't like something: chotto kuchi ni awanakute. Shou ni au is for activities, not food.

example.romaji: kore, kuchi ni au ka wakannai kedo, tabete mite.
example.ja: これ、口に合うかわかんないけど、食べてみて。
example.english: Not sure you'll like it, but give it a try.

examplePolite.romaji: okuchi ni au ka wakarimasen ga, douzo.
examplePolite.ja: お口に合うかわかりませんが、どうぞ。
examplePolite.english: I'm not sure it'll be to your taste, but please have some.

vetted.notes: Polite with o: okuchi ni au; plain way: suki ka wakannai (not sure you'll like it).

vetted.english: a loner who goes their own way

example.ja: 今日は本当に踏んだり蹴ったりだよ。
example.english: Today's been one thing after another.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hontou ni fundari kettari deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は本当に踏んだり蹴ったりでした。
examplePolite.english: Today was one thing after another.

vetted.notes: Plain alternative: tsuitenai (I'm out of luck).

vetted.kana: さんどめのしょうじき
vetted.english: the third try will be the one
vetted.use: Said before a third attempt at an exam, a confession or a game, or after it finally works: kondo koso sandome no shoujiki da. It is the hopeful answer to nido aru koto wa sando aru.

example.romaji: kondo koso sandome no shoujiki da!
example.ja: 今度こそ三度目の正直だ！
example.english: Third time's the charm!

examplePolite.romaji: sandome no shoujiki de, yatto goukaku shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 三度目の正直で、やっと合格しました。
examplePolite.english: Third time lucky, I finally passed.

vetted.english: a pitifully small amount (usually of money)
vetted.use: The stock complaint about pay, bonuses, pensions or interest, often as suzume no namida hodo: boonasu wa suzume no namida hodo datta. Mostly about money, though any tiny amount can qualify.

example.romaji: boonasu, suzume no namida datta yo.
example.ja: ボーナス、雀の涙だったよ。
example.english: My bonus was a pittance.

examplePolite.romaji: boonasu wa suzume no namida deshita.
examplePolite.ja: ボーナスは雀の涙でした。
examplePolite.english: The bonus was next to nothing.

vetted.notes: Plain alternative: hon no sukoshi (just a tiny bit).

vetted.politeJa: 願ってもないことです
vetted.english: better than you could have hoped for, most welcome
vetted.literal: not (to be had) even by wishing
vetted.use: Almost always before a noun: negatte mo nai chansu / hanashi (a chance you couldn't have hoped for), or as sore wa negatte mo nai koto da. Also said on its own as a delighted reply to an offer. Said when an offer or a bit of luck is better than you'd dared to hope.

example.romaji: sore, negatte mo nai chansu jan!
example.ja: それ、願ってもないチャンスじゃん！
example.english: You couldn't ask for a better chance!

examplePolite.romaji: negatte mo nai ohanashi desu.
examplePolite.ja: 願ってもないお話です。
examplePolite.english: That's more than I could have hoped for.

vetted.english: take proper responsibility; draw a clear line
vetted.use: Two everyday uses: owning up to a mess properly, often by apologising or resigning (kejime o tsukenai to), and keeping things clearly apart, like work and private life (koushi no kejime). In dramas it's often a demand or vow to settle accounts: ore ga kejime o tsukeru (I'll settle this myself). keri o tsukeru ends a matter; kejime is about doing it properly.

example.romaji: kono ken wa chanto kejime tsukenai to.
example.ja: この件はちゃんとけじめつけないと。
example.english: I need to take proper responsibility for this.

examplePolite.romaji: kono ken wa kichinto kejime o tsukemasu.
examplePolite.ja: この件はきちんとけじめをつけます。
examplePolite.english: I'll take proper responsibility for this matter.

vetted.notes: kejime o tsukero! is a rough demand (in yakuza dramas, a threat). koushi no kejime: keeping work and private life apart.

vetted.english: a sweet deal, an easy-money offer (usually doubted)
vetted.use: Said about deals, jobs and investments that promise easy gain. The person pitching says it straight (umai hanashi nan da yo), and everyone else usually doubts it: sonna umai hanashi aru wake nai (there's no way that's real), or umai hanashi ni wa ura ga aru (every sweet deal has a catch).

example.romaji: sonna umai hanashi, aru wake nai jan.
example.ja: そんなうまい話、あるわけないじゃん。
example.english: There's no way a deal that good is real.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna umai hanashi wa nai to omoimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんなうまい話はないと思いますよ。
examplePolite.english: I doubt a deal that good really exists.

vetted.notes: Same thing, very common casually: oishii hanashi. Saying: umai hanashi ni wa ura ga aru (a sweet deal always has a catch).

blocks.label: Enough already
blocks.rationale: Outbursts telling someone they have gone too far, from 'knock it off' to 'fine, do what you want'.
blocks.interference: kanben shite vs katte ni shite (both -te pleas: spare me vs do as you like); ii kagen ni shite vs ni mo hodo ga aru (both 'too far').

blocks.label: Getting angry
blocks.rationale: Shades of anger, from mild dislike and disgust to snapping; a natural six.
blocks.interference: katto naru vs kachin to kuru (both sound words: snap vs stung by a remark); hara ga tatsu vs atama ni kuru (belly vs head for the same anger).

blocks.label: In the mood
blocks.rationale: Being willing or not to do something: change your mind, feel like it, not keen, feel bad doing it.
blocks.interference: All ki ga + verb: ki ga noranai (not in the mood) vs ki ga susumanai (reluctant), ki ga muku is the positive.

blocks.label: At wit's end
blocks.rationale: Worn down by a situation: driven crazy, stifled, sick of it, lost, reckless.
blocks.interference: iki ga tsumaru vs iyake ga sasu (similar sound, stifled vs sick of it); tohou ni kureru (at a loss) vs yake ni naru (reckless).

blocks.label: Shock and nerves
blocks.rationale: Creepy, scary or overwhelming moments, and bracing yourself for them.
blocks.interference: kimi ga warui (creepy) vs shinzou ni warui (gave me a scare): both '... warui'.

blocks.label: Feeling better
blocks.rationale: Relief and the gloom lifting: satisfied, at ease, distracted, refreshed, burden lifted.
blocks.interference: ki ga hareru (gloom lifts) vs ki ga magireru (mind taken off it); ki ga sumu (satisfied) vs ki ga raku (at ease).

blocks.label: Cooling off
blocks.rationale: Getting worked up versus calming down and loosening up; a natural three.
blocks.interference: atama o hiyasu (cool off) vs atama ni kuru in Getting angry; kata no chikara o nuku vs kata no ni ga oriru in Feeling better.

blocks.label: Pride, envy, gloating
blocks.rationale: Feelings about other people: proud of them, jealous over them, glad they got what they deserved.
blocks.interference: zamaa miro (to their face) vs ii kimi (about them); ii kimi shares kimi with kimi ga warui.

blocks.label: Feeling down
blocks.rationale: Low spirits: depressed, brooding, discouraged, dreading it.
blocks.interference: ki ga meiru (depressing) vs ki ga omoi (dread it); particles differ: ki o otosu, ki ni yamu.

blocks.label: Embarrassment
blocks.rationale: Self-conscious feelings: it shows on your face, sheepish, it stings to hear, want to disappear.
blocks.interference: kimari ga warui (sheepish) vs the other '... warui' idioms (kimi ga warui, munakuso warui).

blocks.label: Moved
blocks.rationale: Strong feelings in the chest: heartache, being moved, overwhelmed; a natural three.
blocks.interference: mune ga itamu (it pains me) vs mune ga ippai (overwhelmed): same opening, opposite tone.

blocks.label: Kind or nasty
blocks.rationale: How someone treats others, good or bad: thoughtful, trusting, really nasty, teasingly mean.
blocks.interference: hito ga ii and hito ga warui are not opposites: warui is a teasing 'that's mean', while tachi ga warui is truly nasty. ki ga kiku can be mistaken for the literal ki ga tsuku (notice).

blocks.label: Talk and secrets
blocks.rationale: The kuchi set for how someone talks: all talk, keeps secrets, sharp-tongued, blabs, smooth talker.
blocks.interference: kuchi ga katai (discreet) and kuchi ga karui (blabs) differ by one sound. kuchi ga warui (harsh) contrasts with kuchi ga umai (smooth). kuchi ni au (to one's taste) is in Tastes and likeness.

blocks.label: Smart or crazy
blocks.rationale: What someone's head is like: off its hinges, sharp, a quick thinker, quick to pick things up.
blocks.interference: atama ga kireru (sharp) is easy to confuse with plain kireru (snap) and with atama ga okashii (crazy). atama no kaiten ga hayai (fast thinker) and nomikomi ga hayai (fast learner) both end in ga hayai.

blocks.label: Skill and judgement
blocks.rationale: How capable someone is: a poor judge, skilled hands, shrewd, savvy.
blocks.interference: miru me ga nai (poor judge, criticism) and nukeme ga nai (shrewd, praise) share 'ga nai' but are opposite in tone. youryou ga ii can hint at cutting corners; ude ga ii never does.

blocks.label: Immature
blocks.rationale: Faults you scold someone for: selfish, too old for this, dithering, quitting after three days.
blocks.interference: ii toshi shite and ii kagen ni shite (mood) are both scolding lines that start with ii. jibun katte (selfish) can be mixed up with katte ni shite (suit yourself).

blocks.label: In a group
blocks.rationale: What someone is like with other people: the loner, the generous one, the forgiving one, the fun one, the carer.
blocks.interference: kimae ga ii (open-handed with money) and kokoro ga hiroi (forgiving) both translate as 'generous'. kimae, nori and mendoumi all take ga ii.

blocks.label: Stubborn
blocks.rationale: Won't bend: won't listen, won't give up, proud, won't make exceptions, rigid thinking.
blocks.interference: atama ga katai (rigid) can be confused with kuchi ga katai (discreet). iji o haru (out of pride) can be confused with mie o haru (showing off). kiku mimi o motanai (won't listen) and yuuzuu ga kikanai (won't bend) share kiku/kikanai.

blocks.label: Hidden side
blocks.rationale: The person behind the surface: not what they look like, a different person, scheming, faking sweetness, good at heart.
blocks.interference: hara ga kuroi (secretly scheming) vs neko o kaburu (faking innocence). ne wa ii can be mixed up with hito ga ii. hito ga kawaru (become a different person) vs ki ga kawaru (change your mind).

blocks.label: Tastes and likeness
blocks.rationale: What suits whom and who is alike: to one's taste, suits one's nature, alike in character, identical, everyone differs.
blocks.interference: kuchi ni au (suits one's palate) and shou ni au (suits one's nature) both end in ni au. nita mono doushi (alike in character) vs uri futatsu (alike in looks).

blocks.label: Proud or humble
blocks.rationale: Ego in three: talking down, showing off, staying humble.
blocks.interference: ue kara mesen (looking down from above) is the opposite of koshi ga hikui (keeping your hips low). mie o haru can be confused with iji o haru in Stubborn.

blocks.label: Temper
blocks.rationale: The ki ga set for temperament: feisty, hasty, timid, short-tempered, plus caving under pressure.
blocks.interference: ki ga hayai (jumping the gun) vs ki ga mijikai (impatient). ki ga tsuyoi and ki ga yowai are opposites. ki ga yowai (timid) vs oshi ni yowai (caves when pushed).

blocks.label: Lending a hand
blocks.rationale: Offering and giving help, from a quick hand to joining forces.
blocks.interference: te o kasu (a quick hand) vs chikara o kasu (back something bigger) share kasu; chikara ni naru (be there for someone) vs chikara o awaseru (join forces) share chikara.

blocks.label: Dealing with people
blocks.rationale: How you treat someone: obey them, take them on, speak to them, count on them.
blocks.interference: iu koto o kiku (obey) vs kuchi o kiku (be on speaking terms) both end in kiku; aite ni suru (bother with) vs ate ni suru (count on) differ by one sound.

blocks.label: Butting in
blocks.rationale: Getting your hand, mouth or neck into someone else's business, plus the retort to it.
blocks.interference: te o dasu (lay a finger on, get mixed up in) vs kuchi o dasu (butt in) swap only the body part; kao o dasu (show up) is in At a get-together.

blocks.label: Owing favours
blocks.rationale: Asking for, accepting and owing favours.
blocks.interference: kari ga aru (I owe you one) is a debt to repay while on ni kiru (I'm deeply grateful) is thanks; okotoba ni amaete accepts an offer, isshou no onegai begs for one.

blocks.label: Having someone's back
blocks.rationale: Caring about someone, urging them on and taking their side.
blocks.interference: ki ni kakeru (look out for someone) sounds like ki ni kakaru / ki ni suru elsewhere; senaka o osu (push them to go for it) vs kata o motsu (take their side).

blocks.label: Squaring up
blocks.rationale: Rough lines in a confrontation: blaming both sides, brushing off, challenging, picking a fight.
blocks.interference: dotchi mo dotchi (both as bad) vs shitta kotcha nai (not my problem) are both casual put-downs; kenka o uru (pick a fight) vs teki ni mawasu (make an enemy) in Bad blood; keep shitta kotcha nai and nanisama no tsumori casual only.

blocks.label: Clicking and fancying
blocks.rationale: Whether two people get on, and whether someone is into you.
blocks.interference: ki ga au (get along) vs ki ga aru (fancy someone) differ by one sound, and ki o hiku (catch their eye) is a third ki frame; myaku ga aru (there's a chance) is the sign, not the feeling.

blocks.label: Being a burden
blocks.rationale: Being the one who holds others back, or the one who has to put up with it.
blocks.interference: ashi o hipparu (drag down) vs ashidematoi ni naru (be dead weight) both involve legs; sewa ga yakeru describes the handful, shirinugui o suru is cleaning up after them.

blocks.label: Letting things go
blocks.rationale: Forgiving or overlooking after a falling-out, and the no-hard-feelings line.
blocks.interference: nakatta koto ni suru (pretend it never happened), oome ni miru (let it slide) and mizu ni nagasu (forgive and forget) are near-synonyms; mizu ni nagasu vs mizu o sasu (spoil the mood) share mizu.

blocks.label: Bad blood
blocks.rationale: Rubbing people the wrong way, from offence to a new enemy or a lasting grudge.
blocks.interference: ki o waruku suru (they take offence) vs ki ni sawaru (it grates on them) differ in who is hurt; don't merge ki ni sawaru with ki ni suru / ki ni naru; ne ni motsu (hold a grudge) is the opposite of mizu ni nagasu in Letting things go.

blocks.label: At a get-together
blocks.rationale: Showing up to a gathering, dampening the mood and wrapping it up.
blocks.interference: kao o dasu (show up) vs te o dasu / kuchi o dasu in Butting in; mizu o sasu (spoil the mood) vs mizu ni nagasu (forgive and forget) share mizu.

blocks.label: Close and distant
blocks.rationale: Who is inside your circle and how far you let them in.
blocks.interference: aka no tanin (a complete stranger) vs tanin gyougi (too formal with someone close) share tanin; kokoro o hiraku (open up) is the opposite of kyori o oku (keep your distance).

blocks.label: Who you know
blocks.rationale: Ties, networks and the small-world saying.
blocks.interference: en o kiru (cut ties) vs en ga aru (be meant to be) share en; kao ga hiroi (know lots of people) is not kao o dasu (show up).

blocks.label: Couples
blocks.rationale: Romantic relationships, from crossing the line to bickering like an old married couple.
blocks.interference: issen o koeru (sleep together, go too far) vs yori o modosu (get back together); kenka suru hodo naka ga ii vs kenka o uru (pick a fight) in Squaring up.

blocks.label: Reading people
blocks.rationale: Sensing what others feel or want without being told.
blocks.interference: kuuki o yomu (read the room) vs kaoiro o ukagau (anxiously watch one person's mood); aite no mi ni naru is empathy, ishin denshin is understanding each other without words.

blocks.label: Under someone's thumb
blocks.rationale: Deferring to someone with power over you: flattering, humouring, unable to push back.
blocks.interference: goma o suru (suck up for gain) vs kigen o toru (keep someone in a good mood); atama ga agaranai (can't stand up to them) vs shiri ni shikareru (bossed around by your wife).

blocks.label: Saying it
blocks.rationale: The core 'say it' idioms: mentioning something, voicing it, and 'needless to say'.
blocks.interference: kuchi ni suru and kuchi ni dasu both mean say aloud; kuchi ni suru is also formal 'eat or drink', while kuchi ni dasu stresses finally voicing what was held in.

blocks.label: Hearing
blocks.rationale: The mimi idioms for hearing about something and for listening.
blocks.interference: mimi ni suru (you hear it) vs mimi ni hairu (word reaches you) vs komimi ni hasamu (you catch it in passing); mimi o kasu is listening, and is mostly said in the negative.

blocks.label: About the talk
blocks.rationale: Four fixed hanashi remarks about where a discussion stands.
blocks.interference: hanashi ga chigau (not what we agreed) vs hanashi wa betsu (a separate matter); hanashi ni naranai (hopeless) vs hanashi ga hayai (that makes it easy).

blocks.label: Wrong words
blocks.rationale: Shutting down what someone said, and walking back what you said yourself.
blocks.interference: baka iwanaide (don't talk nonsense) vs engi demo nai (don't jinx it); kotoba no aya (just a figure of speech) vs kokoro ni mo nai koto o iu (said in anger, not meant).

blocks.label: Straight or soft
blocks.rationale: Talking things out directly with someone, set against softening it or being brutally blunt.
blocks.interference: hanashi o tsukeru (settle a matter) vs hara o watte hanasu (open up honestly); oburaato ni tsutsumu (soften it) vs mi mo futa mo nai (brutally blunt); tantou chokunyuu = get to the point, men to mukatte = to someone's face.

blocks.label: Look who's talking
blocks.rationale: Calling out someone's nerve or hypocrisy, and admitting your own.
blocks.interference: yoku iu yo and ii dokyou shiteru both come out as 'you've got some nerve': yoku iu yo scoffs at a remark, ii dokyou shiteru is a veiled warning; kotchi no serifu throws their words back, hito no koto ienai turns it on yourself, tana ni ageru describes the hypocrisy.

blocks.label: Secrets
blocks.rationale: Sharing a secret, letting it slip, playing dumb, and keeping it for life.
blocks.interference: kuchi ga suberu (let it slip) vs shira o kiru (play dumb about what you know); koko dake no hanashi shares a secret, hakaba made motte iku keeps one forever.

blocks.label: Conversation flow
blocks.rationale: Moments inside a conversation: butting in, derailing, the subject walking in, awkward silence.
blocks.interference: kuchi o hasamu (butt in) vs hanashi no koshi o oru (derail someone mid-story); ma ga motanai is running out of things to say, not interrupting.

blocks.label: Warned you
blocks.rationale: Warning ahead, telling someone again and again, and 'I told you so' afterwards.
blocks.interference: nen o osu (remind to make sure) vs kugi o sasu (stern warning in advance); mimi ni tako ga dekiru is the listener's complaint, kuchi o suppaku shite iu the speaker's.

blocks.label: Lies and big talk
blocks.rationale: Lying, bragging and stretching the truth, from flat lies to fudged ages.
blocks.interference: makka na uso (a flat lie) vs uso mo houben (a white lie is sometimes fine); hanashi o moru pads a story, ooguchi o tataku brags about what you'll do, saba o yomu fudges a number.

blocks.label: Comebacks and digs
blocks.rationale: Verbal sparring: sniping, winning and losing the exchange.
blocks.interference: ippon torareta (you got me) vs guu no ne mo denai (no comeback at all); aa ieba kou iu (always has a retort) vs hitokoto ooi (always one remark too many); kechi o tsukeru is not the single word kechi (stingy).

blocks.label: Giving it everything
blocks.rationale: Four ways to say you are putting everything into something, from the everyday isshou kenmei to the dramatic shinu ki de.
blocks.interference: isshou kenmei is ordinary effort and shinu ki de is life-or-death; kiai o ireru means psyching yourself up, and nani ga nandemo means 'whatever it takes'.

blocks.label: Work and breaks
blocks.rationale: The arc of a workload: a mountain to do, no end in sight, a good place to stop, and a breather.
blocks.interference: kiri ga nai and kiri ga ii share kiri with opposite meanings: 'there's no end to it' versus 'a good point to stop'.

blocks.label: Learning a skill
blocks.rationale: Progress on something new: start on it, get the knack, hit a wall, keep adding up, until it is yours.
blocks.interference: mi ni tsukeru and te o tsukeru share tsukeru: mi means making a skill your own, while te means starting on a task (or touching food or money).

blocks.label: Against the clock
blocks.rationale: Time running out or slipping away: over in no time, stalling for time, and a deadline finally lighting a fire.
blocks.interference: none

blocks.label: Too much to handle
blocks.rationale: Something beyond you: out of control, daunting, too heavy a responsibility, or an opponent you cannot match.
blocks.interference: ha ga tatanai and tachiuchi dekinai both mean 'no match for' (ha is also used for a problem you can't crack, tachiuchi for rivals); te ni oenai means out of control, and ni ga omoi means too much responsibility.

blocks.label: Not right now
blocks.rationale: Whether you are free at this moment: tied up, hands full, no time for that, or finally free.
blocks.interference: te ga hanasenai (can't step away) and te ga aku (be free) use the same te ga frame with opposite meanings; te ippai is about overall capacity, not this one moment.

blocks.label: Keeping your nerve
blocks.rationale: Motivation rising and falling: warming to it, 'you can do it', talking of quitting, and finally giving up inside.
blocks.interference: yowane o haku means saying aloud that you can't take it, while kokoro ga oreru means the will itself giving way inside.

blocks.label: Slacking off
blocks.rationale: The opposite of effort: half-hearted, easing off, and cutting corners.
blocks.interference: ki o nuku and te o nuku differ by one word: ki means letting your attention slip (often a warning), while te means cutting corners on purpose.

blocks.label: Hard work or easy
blocks.rationale: How much effort a task takes, from hard work, high-maintenance and elaborately made to 'happy to help' and child's play.
blocks.interference: te ga kakaru (needs a lot of looking after) and te ga komu (made with real care) share te ga; oyasui goyou is a reply to a request, while asameshi mae describes a task.

blocks.label: Swamped
blocks.rationale: Overloaded for days: can't keep it up, can't get around to things, crazy busy, desperate for any help.
blocks.interference: te ga mawaranai and me ga mawaru both use mawaru: te means you can't get around to it, while me means dizzy or crazy busy.

blocks.label: Having an idea
blocks.rationale: Knowing or not knowing who, why or what: the two most-said idioms of the topic (357, 251) plus the 'I know full well' answer.
blocks.interference: kentou mo tsukanai (not even a guess) and kokoroatari ga nai (nothing comes to mind) both come out as 'no idea'; hyaku mo shouchi is 'I know', usually followed by a 'but'.

blocks.label: Eyes on it
blocks.rationale: Where your eyes are held: not taking them off, setting them on someone, things catching them, being glued, keeping watch.
blocks.interference: me ni tsuku (it catches your eye) vs me o tsukeru (you single someone out): the particle flips who acts; me o hanasu na (don't look away) and me o hikaraseru (keep a sharp eye) both mean watching closely.

blocks.label: Doesn't add up
blocks.rationale: Judging whether something makes sense, from baffling to logical but it still won't sit right.
blocks.interference: suji ga tooru (it holds together) vs tsujitsuma ga awanai (the details clash); wake ga wakaranai (makes no sense) vs nani ga nan da ka wakaranai (lost about what's going on); fu ni ochinai is a feeling that persists even when the logic works.

blocks.label: Not yourself
blocks.rationale: Someone, or your own head, not working the way it usually does.
blocks.interference: dou ka shiteru (you've lost it) and dou iu kaze no fukimawashi (what's got into you, often at sudden kindness) both open with dou; atama ga mawaranai blurs with kuchi ga mawaranai and the busy list's te ga mawaranai.

blocks.label: Careful or careless
blocks.rationale: How much attention you give something: looking it over and minding others vs underrating it or putting it second.
blocks.interference: amaku miru (underrate someone or something) vs kangae ga amai (your own plan is naive): both built on amai; me o toosu is a once-through read, not a close inspection.

blocks.label: Mind elsewhere
blocks.rationale: Attention stuck on one thing or scattered, so you're not really present.
blocks.interference: ki ga chiru (scattered by your surroundings) vs ki o torareru (pulled away by one thing); atama kara hanarenai (can't stop thinking of it) and atama ga ippai (room for nothing else) both mean preoccupied; uwa no sora is how it looks from outside.

blocks.label: Looking away
blocks.rationale: Choosing not to see something, plus missing what's right under your nose.
blocks.interference: me o tsuburu (let it slide) vs me o somukeru (refuse to face it) vs mite minu furi (pretend you didn't see); toudai moto kurashi is overlooking by accident, not by choice.

blocks.label: Hunches and surprises
blocks.rationale: Feelings about what's coming: it's nothing, a premonition, never saw it coming, a revelation.
blocks.interference: ki no sei (just your imagination) vs mushi no shirase (a feeling that proved right); omoi mo yoranai and yume ni mo omowanakatta both mean 'never imagined'.

blocks.label: Fair point
blocks.rationale: Granting that someone's reaction or guess makes sense.
blocks.interference: muri mo nai (no wonder, understandable) vs ichiri aru (you have a point); ii sen itteru means close to the right answer, not agreement.

blocks.label: Comes to mind
blocks.rationale: Ideas and pictures surfacing, or almost surfacing.
blocks.interference: atama ni ukabu (an idea comes to mind) vs me ni ukabu (you can picture it); pin to kuru means it clicks or rings a bell, and pin to konai means it doesn't grab you.

blocks.label: Obvious or hidden
blocks.rationale: Things in plain sight vs things below the surface.
blocks.interference: me ni mieteru (the outcome is predictable) vs ichimoku ryouzen (clear at a glance) vs kao ni kaite aru (your feelings show); ura ga aru (a hidden catch, negative) vs oku ga fukai (hidden depth, positive).

blocks.label: Believing it
blocks.rationale: How much of what you hear you believe, from swallowing it whole to not falling for it.
blocks.interference: ma ni ukeru (take it seriously) vs unomi ni suru (swallow it uncritically); sono te ni wa noranai rejects a trick outright, while hanshin hangi only half believes.

blocks.label: Can't resist
blocks.rationale: Desire, greed and curiosity pulling at your attention.
blocks.interference: me ga nai (crazy about it, fondly) vs me ga kuramu (blinded by greed): both start me ga, and the character list's miru me ga nai (poor judge) sounds alike; kuse ni naru describes the moreish thing, me ga nai describes you.

blocks.label: Gains and windfalls
blocks.rationale: Good things coming your way, from simply getting hold of something to luck that falls in your lap.
blocks.interference: te ni ireru (you get it) vs te ni hairu (it comes to you) is a transitive/intransitive pair; tanabota is unearned luck, negatte mo nai is a chance better than you'd hoped for.

blocks.label: A rough time
blocks.rationale: Going through something bad, from one nasty experience to one blow after another.
blocks.interference: hidoi me ni au (an awful time) vs itai me ni au (paying for a mistake) share me ni au; ma ga warui (bad timing) sounds like ma ga sashita (a sudden lapse) in Getting carried away.

blocks.label: Out of a job
blocks.rationale: Being fired, firing someone, or leaving a shady line of work behind.
blocks.interference: kubi ni naru (you get fired) vs kubi ni suru (you fire someone); ashi o arau is quitting by choice, not being fired.

blocks.label: Making a move
blocks.rationale: Moves and timing against the other side: acting, having no other option, getting in first or being beaten to it.
blocks.interference: te o utsu (take action, settle for) vs sente o utsu (move first); saki o kosareru is the losing end of sente o utsu, and hayai mono gachi is the rule behind both.

blocks.label: The short end
blocks.rationale: Coming off worse: stuck with a chore, playing into someone's hands, taking the blame, drawing the worst lot.
blocks.interference: hame ni naru (stuck doing it) shares hame with hame o hazusu (let loose) in Getting carried away; binbou kuji o hiku is about being the unlucky one, hame ni naru about the chore itself.

blocks.label: Comes back on you
blocks.rationale: Bad outcomes you brought on yourself: your own fault, the bill coming due, digging your own grave, punishment, a plan backfiring.
blocks.interference: jigou jitoku (your own fault) vs bachi ga ataru (punished from above) vs tsuke ga mawatte kuru (it catches up later); boketsu o horu (you make it worse for yourself) vs urame ni deru (a plan has the opposite effect).

blocks.label: Getting carried away
blocks.rationale: Losing your restraint: getting cocky, going overboard, getting full of yourself, a sudden lapse.
blocks.interference: choushi ni noru (cocky, can be playful) vs ii ki ni naru (smug, a sharper rebuke); ma ga sashita (a lapse) vs ma ga warui (bad timing) in A rough time.

blocks.label: Closing the matter
blocks.rationale: Bringing a matter to an end: settling it, declaring it done, owning it properly.
blocks.interference: keri o tsukeru (finish it off) vs kejime o tsukeru (take responsibility, draw a line) share o tsukeru; ikken rakuchaku is said once it's done.

blocks.label: All for nothing
blocks.rationale: Effort or chances that are lost, progress wiped out, and being too late to fix it.
blocks.interference: mizu no awa (effort comes to nothing) vs bou ni furu (you throw something away yourself); torikaeshi ga tsukanai (can't be undone) vs ato no matsuri (too late to act).

blocks.label: Bound to happen
blocks.rationale: Remarks about what is sure to come, or come again: a matter of time, a repeat failure, threes, experts slipping.
blocks.interference: nido aru koto wa sando aru (bad luck repeats) vs sandome no shoujiki (the third try works) predict opposite thirds; ni no mai is repeating one particular past failure.

blocks.label: Taking a gamble
blocks.rationale: Taking a chance: trying with nothing to lose, betting everything, risky moves, offers that look too good.
blocks.interference: dame moto (nothing to lose) vs ichi ka bachi ka (all or nothing); its bachi is unrelated to bachi ga ataru (punishment) in Comes back on you.

blocks.label: Whatever happens
blocks.rationale: Taking outcomes calmly, before or after they happen.
blocks.interference: sono toki wa sono toki (before the fact: deal with it then) vs kekka oorai (after the fact: it worked out); naru you ni naru is a general shrug.

blocks.label: Close calls
blocks.rationale: Coming through danger: the worst passing, a near miss, a razor-thin margin, the one lucky part of a bad situation.
blocks.interference: kiki ippatsu (a near disaster) vs kami hitoe (a razor-thin gap, often between winning and losing); yama o kosu is the crisis passing, not a near miss.

blocks.label: Worth the money
blocks.rationale: Money and value: not worth it, costs adding up, getting your money back, a pitiful sum.
blocks.interference: wari ni awanai (doesn't pay) vs moto o toru (get your money's worth); baka ni naranai (costs add up) vs suzume no namida (a tiny amount).

stages.name: Stage 1
stages.summary: Tell someone to knock it off, say you're angry or not in the mood, offer or ask for help, call people kind, clever or loose-lipped, say something makes no sense, and talk about luck, bad times and getting fired.

stages.name: Stage 2
stages.summary: Say you're at your wit's end or shaken up, call people skilled, immature or easygoing, point out hypocrisy, say what's too much to handle, and talk about who you click with, who's a burden and getting the short end.

stages.name: Stage 3
stages.summary: Say you feel better or need to cool off, describe stubborn or two-faced people, let things go or hold a grudge, keep a secret, and talk about being busy, hunches, getting carried away and wasted effort.

stages.name: Stage 4
stages.summary: Say you're down, embarrassed or moved, talk about couples, connections and who's under whose thumb, call out lies and say you warned them, and say whether a gamble or a purchase was worth it.
